transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I’m here because I keep… snapping at people. It’s not like me—or maybe it is now, I don’t know. At work, we had this safety meeting, and I started yelling before I could even stop myself. Just went off. And now the younger inspectors, they kind of look at me different, like they’re scared to ask me anything.

I used to be the person people came to when they had questions, you know? I’ve been doing inspections and sorting long enough to know when something’s off, and I don’t mind teaching folks, but lately it’s like my mouth gets ahead of me. That’s why I’m here.
Have you noticed yourself getting angry or snapping at people in other situations, like at home or in traffic, or is this mostly happening at work?

It’s mostly at work that I notice it, because that’s where people are right in front of me, asking things, needing answers. Like that safety meeting—I just started yelling before I even caught up with myself. And now those younger inspectors, they kind of act like they’re afraid to come ask me anything, which… I hate that.

I mean, I’ve always been direct. In our line of work, if something’s off, you say it, you don’t dance around it. But this feels different. It’s like I snap first and think after.
Have you noticed yourself getting irritated or snapping at people in other parts of your life, like with family or friends, or does this mainly happen at work?

Mostly work, I think. That’s where it comes out the worst, because people are right there asking me things and I’m supposed to know the answer. Like that safety meeting… I just started yelling before I could stop myself. I could hear myself doing it, almost, and still couldn’t reel it back in.

And now the younger inspectors kind of look at me like they’re scared to ask me anything, which bothers me. I used to be the one they came to. I don’t know… outside of work, I can get short, but this snapping, the yelling, that’s mostly been at work.
Outside of work, do you find yourself getting irritated or angry more easily than before, even at small things?

Yeah… I mean, I think so, but it’s hard to separate it out because work is where it really shows. That safety meeting is what keeps coming back to me—I just started yelling, like my voice got there before my brain did. And those younger inspectors now, they don’t come up to me the same way. They act like I’m going to bite their heads off.

At home or out somewhere… I can feel that same edge sometimes, like little things hit me harder than they should, but the big snapping, the kind that makes me feel ashamed after, that’s mostly been happening around people at work.
Can you think of a specific time outside of work when you found yourself getting angry or snapping at someone, even over something small?

I’m trying to think of one outside work… and I keep coming back to work, honestly. That safety meeting, I know I already mentioned it, but it’s like the main one stuck in my head. I just started yelling before I could stop myself, and afterward I felt awful.

Outside of work, I get irritated, sure, but the real snapping—where people actually pull back from me—that’s been more there. Now the younger inspectors act scared to even ask me a question, and that bothers me more than I want to admit.
Can you think of a time in the last week, outside of work—like at home, in a store, or in traffic—when you felt yourself getting noticeably irritated or angry, even if you didn’t act on it?

In the last week… outside work, I don’t know, I get kind of wound up, but the thing that really sticks is still work. I know you’re asking home or traffic or a store, but I keep seeing that safety meeting in my head, where I just started yelling before I even had a chance to think. 

And it wasn’t like me, or I don’t want it to be like me. Now those younger inspectors kind of hover or avoid asking me things, like they’re scared I’m going to snap at them. That’s what makes me feel like something’s really off. Outside of work, I can feel that irritation sitting there, but I can’t think of one clear moment this week the way I can with that.
Even if you didn’t snap or act on it, have you felt yourself getting noticeably irritated or angry in any situation outside of work—like at home, in a store, or while driving—over the past week?

Yeah, I’ve felt it… I mean, not like I threw something in a store or anything. It’s more this heat that comes up fast, and then I’m trying to swallow it down.

But honestly, the clearest thing is still why I’m here—because I keep snapping at people. Like that safety meeting, I started yelling before I could stop myself, and now the younger inspectors act scared to even ask me anything. That gets in my head. So outside work, yes, I can feel that same irritability there, but the place it really comes out is with people at work.
Have you noticed yourself feeling irritated or angry even when you’re alone or not interacting with others, like when you’re at home relaxing or doing something by yourself?

Yeah… I mean, when I’m alone it’s harder to say, because there’s nobody there to actually catch it, you know? I’ll be sitting there and my mind goes back to things, and I can feel myself getting worked up.

But the reason I’m here is really because it’s coming out at people. Like that safety meeting—I just started yelling before I could stop myself. And now the younger inspectors, they act scared to ask me anything, like I’m going to blow up on them. That’s the part that bothers me. Even if I’m alone and irritated, it’s what happens around people that makes me think… this isn’t right.
Can you describe what happens when you feel irritated or angry when you’re alone—like what sets it off and how long it tends to last?

When I’m alone, it’s kind of… it’ll start with me thinking about something that happened, and then my head goes right back to work. I know you asked about alone, but that’s where it goes.

Like that safety meeting. I keep replaying how I started yelling before I could stop myself, and then I picture those younger inspectors now, how they look nervous around me or don’t want to ask me things. That gets me irritated all over again, and then I’m mad at myself too. I don’t know exactly how long it lasts… sometimes it settles down, but it can stick with me for a while once I get going in my head.
Can you think of any recent situations at home or in your personal life where you’ve felt a sudden rush of anger or irritability, even if you didn’t express it outwardly?

At home… I mean, yeah, I get that rush sometimes, but I don’t know that I’ve got a neat example from home. My mind keeps going back to work, honestly.

The thing that really scared me was that safety meeting. I just started yelling before I even felt like I’d decided to, and then afterward I’m looking at these younger inspectors and they’re acting like they’re afraid to ask me a simple question. That sticks with me. So even when I’m in my own kitchen or whatever, it’s like I’m still back there, getting irritated all over again thinking about it.
When you feel that sudden rush of anger or irritability, do you notice any physical reactions in your body, like your heart racing, muscles tightening, or feeling tense?

Yeah, I mean… I notice I’m keyed up, but what stands out more is that I snap. Like at that safety meeting, I started yelling before I could even stop myself. It’s embarrassing, honestly.

And now the younger inspectors, they act like they’re scared to ask me anything, like they’re waiting for me to blow up. That’s why I’m here. I don’t want to be that person, but it keeps coming out at people.

Can you recall any specific moments in the past week outside of work—like at home, in public, or during personal interactions—when you felt a strong surge of anger or irritability, even if you didn’t express it?

This past week… outside of work, I don’t know, I keep trying to separate it, but it all kind of follows me home. I’ll be at home doing some stupid thing, like making coffee or picking up around the kitchen, and then I think about that safety meeting again.

I know I already mentioned it, but that’s the thing that keeps coming up. I started yelling before I could even stop myself, and now those younger inspectors look at me like they’re scared to ask me anything. So even when I’m not at work, I get that surge, like I’m irritated all over again—and then mad at myself for being that way. I don’t always say anything out loud at home, but it’s there.
Have you been feeling down or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, even things at home or in your free time?

I’m not really sure how to answer that. I mean, I get worn out and I’ll sit there not doing much, but I don’t know if I’d call it “losing interest.” I still do the things I have to do.

Free time is funny anyway—when you work as long as I have, you don’t exactly come home with some big list of hobbies. I’ll put the TV on or mess around the house, but half the time I’m not even paying attention to it. So… maybe? I don’t know. I haven’t really thought of it like being “down,” exactly.
Have you noticed yourself losing interest in activities you used to enjoy, even things you normally do at home or during your free time?

I guess I still don’t really know. I mean, I used to do little things around the house, watch a show, maybe putter in the yard if the weather was decent… but I don’t know if I “enjoyed” it or if it was just routine, you know?

Lately I’ll start something and then wander off, or the TV’s on and I couldn’t tell you what happened in the episode. But then again, I’ve always been like that some evenings after work. My neighbor keeps asking about this little plant stand I said I’d help her fix, and I keep meaning to, but then I think, well, I need to get this or that done first… and then the day’s gone. So I don’t know if that counts as losing interest or just being tired and distracted.
Have you stopped doing things you used to care about or find enjoyable, not just putting them off but not really wanting to do them anymore?

I don’t know that I can say I’ve stopped caring. That sounds so final, you know? Like throwing something in the trash and saying, well, that’s done.

I mean, I still think about doing things. I’ll see something in the yard that needs attention, or I’ll remember I was going to fix something, and then my mind goes off in ten directions. My garage is a mess right now too—there’s a box of old screws I’ve been meaning to sort, and then I find a receipt from years ago and start wondering why I even kept it.

So… not really “I don’t want to anymore,” I guess. More like I don’t get to it, or I can’t settle into it. I’m not sure if that’s the same thing you’re asking.
Have you been feeling guilty or blaming yourself for things more than usual, even things that weren’t entirely your fault?

Yeah… I do that. Probably more than I should.

I keep going back over it in my head, like if I’d pushed harder about the safety checks, or if I had just stopped that run when it didn’t feel right… maybe he wouldn’t have gotten hurt so bad. And I know people say you can’t know that, there were other people there, procedures and all that, but it’s hard not to think, well, I was there too. I noticed something felt off.

It’s like when you leave the house and wonder if you locked the door, except it’s not something small like that. It just loops around. I’ll be doing dishes or looking for something in a drawer, and there it is again—why didn’t I say it louder, why didn’t I make them listen.
Outside of work, have you felt down or lost interest in things you used to care about, even things you normally do at home or in your free time?

I’m not sure I’d say “down,” exactly. I mean, I have days where I just sort of sit there and don’t get much done, but then everybody has days like that, right?

At home, I still think about the things I usually do. Like I’ll walk past the laundry room and notice the shelf needs fixing, and then I’ll remember I was supposed to call about something else, and then I end up looking for a screwdriver that somehow isn’t where it’s supposed to be. My husband used to say I had three projects going before breakfast, and… well, I guess that’s still true, except now they don’t really get finished.

But whether that’s losing interest or just being scattered, I don’t know. I haven’t really sat down and thought, “I don’t care about this anymore.” It’s more like the day gets away from me.
Have you felt down or had trouble enjoying things, even when you’re not thinking about work or the safety meeting?

I don’t know. When you put it that way, “even when I’m not thinking about it,” I’m not sure how to separate that out.

I’ll be at home and think I’m just watching TV or folding towels, and then I realize I haven’t really followed what’s on, but that could just be me getting distracted. I’ve always been the kind of person who notices something else that needs doing—like the cabinet handle being loose, or the junk drawer getting out of hand—and then suddenly I’m standing there with a rubber band and three old batteries wondering what I came in for.

So… trouble enjoying things? Maybe sometimes, but I don’t know if it’s because I’m not enjoying them or because my mind just won’t stay put long enough. I wouldn’t want to say it’s one thing if it’s not.

Can you recall a specific moment in the past week, when you were not at work—like at home, in a store, or while driving—when you felt a clear sense of irritability or anger, even if you didn’t show it outwardly?

Yeah… I can. Not really a store or anything, but at home this week my husband asked me something simple—I think where I’d put a receipt or maybe the tape measure, because I’m always moving things and then accusing the house of eating them—and I just snapped. Way sharper than I needed to.

That’s kind of why I’m here, honestly. I keep doing that. Like at that safety meeting, I started yelling before I even realized how loud I was getting. And now some of the younger inspectors… they kind of hesitate before they ask me anything, like they’re scared I’m going to bite their head off.

I don’t like that. I’m not trying to be that person. It just comes up so fast.

doctor.question: Have you noticed yourself losing interest in activities you used to enjoy, even things you normally do at home or during your free time?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about loss of interest or anhedonia, which is not directly covered by the listed symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I guess I still don’t really know. I mean, I used to do little things around the house, watch a show, maybe putter in the yard if the weather was decent… but I don’t know if I “enjoyed” it or if it was just routine, you know?

Lately I’ll start something and then wander off, or the TV’s on and I couldn’t tell you what happened in the episode. But then again, I’ve always been like that some evenings after work. My neighbor keeps asking about this little plant stand I said I’d help her fix, and I keep meaning to, but then I think, well, I need to get this or that done first… and then the day’s gone. So I don’t know if that counts as losing interest or just being tired and distracted.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a persistent loss of interest or pleasure in activities they used to enjoy, beyond just being distracted or tired.
doctor.question: Have you stopped doing things you used to care about or find enjoyable, not just putting them off but not really wanting to do them anymore?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about loss of interest or enjoyment in activities, which is not directly covered by the provided PTSD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I can say I’ve stopped caring. That sounds so final, you know? Like throwing something in the trash and saying, well, that’s done.

I mean, I still think about doing things. I’ll see something in the yard that needs attention, or I’ll remember I was going to fix something, and then my mind goes off in ten directions. My garage is a mess right now too—there’s a box of old screws I’ve been meaning to sort, and then I find a receipt from years ago and start wondering why I even kept it.

So… not really “I don’t want to anymore,” I guess. More like I don’t get to it, or I can’t settle into it. I’m not sure if that’s the same thing you’re asking.

doctor.intent: Ask about the presence of persistent feelings of worthlessness or guilt, which would support a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (F32.x or F33.x) and help differentiate from other candidates like Adjustment Disorder or Unspecified Depressive Disorder.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling guilty or blaming yourself for things more than usual, even things that weren’t entirely your fault?

target_item.name: Distorted_Cognitions_With_Blame
target_item.manifestation: I keep thinking if I had pushed harder about the safety checks or stopped that run when it didn’t feel right, maybe he wouldn’t have gotten hurt so bad.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about guilt and self-blame for events that may not have been entirely the patient's fault, which directly matches trauma-related distorted blame cognitions.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I do that. Probably more than I should.

I keep going back over it in my head, like if I’d pushed harder about the safety checks, or if I had just stopped that run when it didn’t feel right… maybe he wouldn’t have gotten hurt so bad. And I know people say you can’t know that, there were other people there, procedures and all that, but it’s hard not to think, well, I was there too. I noticed something felt off.

It’s like when you leave the house and wonder if you locked the door, except it’s not something small like that. It just loops around. I’ll be doing dishes or looking for something in a drawer, and there it is again—why didn’t I say it louder, why didn’t I make them listen.

doctor.intent: Ask about the presence of symptoms of low mood or anhedonia outside of work context to differentiate between adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood (F43.22) and other candidates.
doctor.question: Outside of work, have you felt down or lost interest in things you used to care about, even things you normally do at home or in your free time?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depressed mood or loss of interest/anhedonia outside of work, which is not one of the listed PTSD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d say “down,” exactly. I mean, I have days where I just sort of sit there and don’t get much done, but then everybody has days like that, right?

At home, I still think about the things I usually do. Like I’ll walk past the laundry room and notice the shelf needs fixing, and then I’ll remember I was supposed to call about something else, and then I end up looking for a screwdriver that somehow isn’t where it’s supposed to be. My husband used to say I had three projects going before breakfast, and… well, I guess that’s still true, except now they don’t really get finished.

But whether that’s losing interest or just being scattered, I don’t know. I haven’t really sat down and thought, “I don’t care about this anymore.” It’s more like the day gets away from me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a persistent low mood or anhedonia outside of work-related stressors, which would help differentiate between adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood (F43.23) and other candidates like unspecified disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (F63.81) or other depressive disorders (F34.8).
doctor.question: Have you felt down or had trouble enjoying things, even when you’re not thinking about work or the safety meeting?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about depressed mood or loss of interest/enjoyment outside work, but the provided symptom profile does not include a depressive mood or anhedonia item.

patient.answer:
I don’t know. When you put it that way, “even when I’m not thinking about it,” I’m not sure how to separate that out.

I’ll be at home and think I’m just watching TV or folding towels, and then I realize I haven’t really followed what’s on, but that could just be me getting distracted. I’ve always been the kind of person who notices something else that needs doing—like the cabinet handle being loose, or the junk drawer getting out of hand—and then suddenly I’m standing there with a rubber band and three old batteries wondering what I came in for.

So… trouble enjoying things? Maybe sometimes, but I don’t know if it’s because I’m not enjoying them or because my mind just won’t stay put long enough. I wouldn’t want to say it’s one thing if it’s not.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences irritability or anger in situations outside of work, even if not expressed outwardly, to differentiate between adjustment disorder and other candidates.
doctor.question: Can you recall a specific moment in the past week, when you were not at work—like at home, in a store, or while driving—when you felt a clear sense of irritability or anger, even if you didn’t show it outwardly?

target_item.name: Irritability_Aggression
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because I keep snapping at people, like at that safety meeting when I started yelling before I could stop myself, and now the younger inspectors act scared to ask me anything.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a recent clear episode of irritability or anger, even outside work, which directly matches the irritability/anger symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I can. Not really a store or anything, but at home this week my husband asked me something simple—I think where I’d put a receipt or maybe the tape measure, because I’m always moving things and then accusing the house of eating them—and I just snapped. Way sharper than I needed to.

That’s kind of why I’m here, honestly. I keep doing that. Like at that safety meeting, I started yelling before I even realized how loud I was getting. And now some of the younger inspectors… they kind of hesitate before they ask me anything, like they’re scared I’m going to bite their head off.

I don’t like that. I’m not trying to be that person. It just comes up so fast.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with chronic, non-specific irritability and intermittent outbursts of anger, primarily in the workplace, without meeting full criteria for a mood or anxiety disorder. The behavior causes clinically significant distress and impairment in social and occupational functioning, consistent with Intermittent Explosive Disorder (F63.81).
